analysis.title: Houston, Do We Have A Problem?
key_insights: Citadel Securities' head of macro strategy (Frank Flight) sees the midterm results as a headwind for the AI investment cycle, a possible accelerator of a diplomatic settlement of the Iran conflict, and a political shift toward the centre ahead of 2028.

Voter backlash against data-centre development adds constraints on the pace of AI infrastructure deployment. 56% of voters called AI and data centres a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, and voters opposed data-centre development in at least 39 of 45 local ballot initiatives.
Around 45 GW across 350 projects in Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Georgia is at risk between 2026-30, including 24 GW in Texas alone.

The report argues the impact on aggregate AI investment should be considerably smaller than the local restrictions suggest, because capital and construction migrate to jurisdictions that accommodate them. Securing alternative sites, power and approvals takes time, so deployment could still be delayed and costs raised, moderating the near-term growth and inflation impulse from construction.

Expected rotation is a 'peak AI capex' theme: out of memory, neoclouds and energy, into staples, healthcare, banks, housing, retail and the hyperscalers themselves (consistent with the firm's Tokenomics 2.0 view). A slower buildout favours those doing the spending over those receiving it.

Hardware suppliers (most pronounced in memory, optical and other semiconductor components) risk component production running ahead of installation, leaving them exposed to order deferrals and excess inventories while usable compute stays scarce.

Cloud businesses already selling energised compute or bringing fully permitted, powered capacity online soon should benefit from delayed competition through utilisation, pricing power and margins. CBRE reports 1.4% vacancy in primary North American markets and 80.4% of capacity under construction already preleased.
Hyperscalers get relief on free cash flow and financing needs if capex slows. Stock selection will depend on exposure to Texas and other jurisdictions with tighter permitting.

For risk assets in aggregate, slower deployment and greater execution risk are adverse. The report argues against treating the election as a clearing event because the swing was larger than expected and implies a harder AI build-out environment.

For rates, risk aversion, a softer near-term investment impulse, possible financing deferrals and lower energy prices favour lower yields. The report cautions against extrapolating to a lasting collapse in spending or issuance.

The Democratic swing was broad across cohorts. Versus 2022, the Republican advantage among men fell from 14 points to zero, among white men from 28 to 12, among white men without a college degree from 46 to 30, among non-college graduates from 12 to 4, and among voters over 65 from 12 to 3. The Democratic margin among women widened from 8 to 18 and among college graduates from 10 to 26.
Citadel links the swing to the Iran war, tariffs, and higher gasoline and diesel prices, which hit rural and Midwest communities in particular.
Prediction markets repriced the 2028 Republican nomination: DeSantis rose from about 4% to about 19%, and Vance fell from about 36% to 31% but remains the favourite.

Centrist Democrats outperformed. Across 17 states with Senate races in both 2024 and 2026, the average Democratic swing versus the 2024 presidential vote was 6.7 points, 3.1 for Sanders-endorsed candidates and 8.1 for those without his endorsement.

The election may raise political urgency to end the Iran war, since Trump and Vance have attributed Republican losses partly to it. The report frames Tehran's leverage as a long, high-strike oil call expiring around the midterms, and sees Tehran possibly monetising its remaining leverage through a settlement.

Oil options show the market removing Iran escalation premium. The three-month option-implied probability of Brent above $120 fell from 23% to 9% since Oct 28, and the one-month probability fell from 27% to 7%. Upside skew flattened across shorter maturities.

Near-term upside tail risk in crude has been sharply reduced.
Slower investment, reduced near-term financing demand, risk aversion and lower energy prices favour lower yields, though not a lasting collapse in spending or issuance.

risk_factors: Slower data-centre construction and greater execution risk for the AI build-out.
Order deferrals and excess inventory for hardware suppliers, mainly memory, optical and other semiconductor components.
Texas and other jurisdictions with tighter permitting restrictions face greater execution risk and delayed revenue timing.
The Iran settlement may not materialise, leaving energy risk premia exposed to renewed escalation.
The election's larger-than-expected swing implies a more challenging AI investment environment, so it may not act as a clearing event for risk assets.
charts_described: Brent 3-month risk-neutral option price distribution (data as of Nov 2026) shows the market curtailing Iran escalation risk probabilities.
Chart on US data-centre development pipeline shows reported power allocated to construction and planned projects by state, in GW.
vol_and_positioning: The Brent option-implied distribution shows the upside premium being removed: 3-month probability of Brent above $120 fell from 23% to 9% since Oct 28, and the 1-month probability from 27% to 7%.
Upside skew in Brent options has flattened across shorter maturities, consistent with the market removing premium for renewed escalation.
Expected equity positioning shift toward a 'peak AI capex' rotation, out of memory, neoclouds and energy and into staples, healthcare, banks, housing, retail and hyperscalers.
geopolitical: Iran war: the midterm result may raise Washington's urgency to negotiate, and Tehran may seek to monetise its remaining leverage through a settlement.
Substantial crude flows are already being sustained through and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump and Vance have attributed Republican midterm losses partly to the Iran conflict, citing higher energy prices and household purchasing-power pressure.
Tariffs and higher gasoline and diesel prices are cited as having undermined the administration's affordability agenda.

tension_points.bull_case: Capital and construction migrate to jurisdictions willing to build, so aggregate AI investment is only modestly affected while compute stays scarce. Operators with energised compute gain pricing power and hyperscalers gain free cash flow relief.
tension_points.bear_case: Slower deployment and greater execution risk hurt hardware suppliers, with component production running ahead of installation and leading to order deferrals and excess inventories. Alternative sites, power and approvals take time, which delays deployment and raises costs.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Compute demand weakening, which would remove the scarcity incentive for capital to migrate to other jurisdictions.

tension_points.bull_case: Washington's urgency and Tehran's incentive to monetise its remaining leverage align, so a diplomatic resolution compresses energy risk premia. Brent options show the premium already being removed.
tension_points.bear_case: Escalation risk persists if no deal comes, and substantial crude flows remain exposed around the Strait of Hormuz.
